topics.name: Mole Concept
topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.description: Solve any Class 11 stoichiometry question — mole, molar mass, empirical formula, molecular formula and equation mole ratios — unaided, with the unit written on every line.

flashcards.q: A mole and a dozen are both counting words. What does each one count, and why does chemistry need a number as large as the mole's?
flashcards.a:
A dozen counts 12 of anything; a mole counts 6.022 × 10²³ of anything. Chemistry needs the
larger word because atoms are far too small to weigh or count one at a time — 18 g of water, one
spoonful, already holds 6.022 × 10²³ molecules. The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance,
so it is a count, not a mass.

flashcards.q: How are the amount in mol, the molar mass and the mass of a sample related, and which one of the three is read off a balance?
flashcards.a:
n = m ÷ M, where m is the sample mass in g, M is the molar mass in g/mol and n is the amount in
mol. Only m is read off a balance. M is built by adding atomic masses, and n is always calculated,
never weighed.

flashcards.q: State the Avogadro constant with its unit.
flashcards.a:
Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. It is a count per mole, so its unit is per mole — it is not a mass and
not a volume.

flashcards.q: Calculate the amount, in mol, in 88 g of carbon dioxide, and write the unit on every line. (C = 12, O = 16 g/mol.)
flashcards.a:
M(CO₂) = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g/mol. n = m ÷ M = 88 g ÷ 44 g/mol = 2 mol. The g cancels with the g in
g/mol, which is the check that the division ran the right way.

flashcards.q: Without notes, write the whole chain that takes a mass in grams all the way to a number of individual molecules.
flashcards.a:
mass in g → divide by the molar mass in g/mol → amount in mol → multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ →
number of molecules, a bare count with no unit. Reverse both operations to walk back the other way.

flashcards.q: A gas cylinder and an iron block hold the same amount of substance in mol. A classmate says they must therefore weigh the same. Where is the reasoning wrong, and what is actually equal?
flashcards.a:
Equal amount in mol means an equal number of particles, not an equal mass, because mass also
depends on the molar mass and iron's is far larger than most gases'. What is equal is the particle
count: both hold n × 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

flashcards.q: A sample of sodium sulphate contains 3.011 × 10²³ formula units. Find its mass. (Na = 23, S = 32, O = 16 g/mol.)
flashcards.a:
n = 3.011 × 10²³ ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 0.5 mol. M(Na₂SO₄) = 2(23) + 32 + 4(16) = 142 g/mol.
m = n × M = 0.5 mol × 142 g/mol = 71 g. Coming from the particle end is a division, never a
multiplication.

flashcards.q: Why can a percentage by mass never be used directly as a number of atoms, and what single operation repairs it?
flashcards.a:
A percentage by mass is a share of the grams, and atoms of different elements have very
different masses — 40 g of carbon holds far fewer atoms than 40 g of hydrogen. Dividing each
element's mass by that element's own atomic mass in g/mol turns masses into amounts in mol, and
only then is the comparison a ratio of atoms.

flashcards.q: A compound is 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16 g/mol.)
flashcards.a:
In 100 g: 40.0 g C, 6.7 g H, 53.3 g O. n(C) = 3.33 mol, n(H) = 6.70 mol, n(O) = 3.33 mol.
Dividing by the smallest, 3.33 mol, gives 1.00 : 2.01 : 1.00, so the empirical formula is CH₂O.

flashcards.q: In the empirical-formula method, what is each element's mass divided by, and what goes wrong if the compound's molar mass is used instead?
flashcards.a:
Each element's mass is divided by that element's own atomic mass in g/mol — carbon by 12,
hydrogen by 1, oxygen by 16. Dividing all of them by one number scales them equally, so the ratio
comes out exactly as it started and the answer is the percentages wearing a disguise.

flashcards.q: A ratio comes out as 1 : 2.50. State the next move and say why that move is allowed while rounding is not.
flashcards.a:
Multiply every number in the ratio by 2, giving 2 : 5. Scaling is allowed because a ratio
compares the numbers to each other, and scaling both leaves that comparison untouched. Rounding
2.50 up to 3 describes a different compound, and is only ever legitimate for measurement noise
such as 1.98 or 2.02.

flashcards.q: A 4.00 g sample of a compound of calcium and chlorine contains 1.44 g of calcium. Find its empirical formula. (Ca = 40, Cl = 35.5 g/mol.)
The empirical formula is a ratio, while the molecular formula is a ______, and the one extra measurement that converts between them is the ______.
flashcards.a:
a count; the molar mass of the compound in g/mol. Then n = M ÷ E, and every subscript is
multiplied by n.

flashcards.q: A hydrocarbon has empirical formula CH₂ and a molar mass of 84 g/mol. Find its molecular formula. (C = 12, H = 1 g/mol.)
flashcards.a:
E(CH₂) = 12 + 2(1) = 14 g/mol. n = M ÷ E = 84 g/mol ÷ 14 g/mol = 6. Every subscript is
multiplied by 6, giving C₆H₁₂, and the check 6(12) + 12(1) = 84 g/mol matches the measurement.

flashcards.q: Methanal, ethanoic acid and glucose all analyse as 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O. Explain how three different substances can give one set of percentages.
flashcards.a:
Percentage composition fixes only the ratio of atoms, which is CH₂O for all three. The
molecules differ in how many of those units they hold: n = 1 for methanal at 30 g/mol, n = 2 for
ethanoic acid at 60 g/mol and n = 6 for glucose at 180 g/mol. Only the molar mass separates them.

flashcards.q: A calculation of n in the molecular-formula method gives 2.5. State what that number means and what to do about it.
flashcards.a:
n counts whole empirical units inside one molecule, so a value of 2.5 is impossible and is never
rounded. It reports that the molar mass is wrong, the percentage data is wrong, or the starting
formula was not the simplest ratio. The data is checked and the calculation is repeated.

flashcards.q: In a balanced equation, what do the coefficients count, and why can a mass in grams never be put straight into that ratio?
flashcards.a:
They count particles, and therefore amounts in mol once every count is multiplied by
6.022 × 10²³. They never count grams, because particles of different substances have different
masses: in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O the particle ratio 2 : 1 is a mass ratio of 4 g : 32 g. A mass has to
become an amount through n = m ÷ M before the ratio can act on it.

flashcards.q: Sodium burns in chlorine: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. Find the mass of sodium chloride formed from 46 g of sodium. (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5 g/mol.)
flashcards.a:
n(Na) = 46 g ÷ 23 g/mol = 2 mol. The ratio Na : NaCl is 2 : 2, so n(NaCl) = 2 mol.
M(NaCl) = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 g/mol, so m = 2 mol × 58.5 g/mol = 117 g.

flashcards.q: Write the four steps that take a mass of one substance to a mass of another through a balanced equation, naming the unit each step ends in.
flashcards.a:
1 — balance the equation and read the coefficients as particles, then as moles. 2 — n(given) =
m ÷ M, in mol. 3 — n(wanted) = n(given) × coefficient of wanted ÷ coefficient of given, still in
mol. 4 — m(wanted) = n × M of the wanted substance, in g. Grams never talk to grams directly.

flashcards.q: Why is an equation balanced by changing the numbers in front rather than the subscripts inside a formula?
flashcards.a:
A subscript is part of the substance's identity — H₂O is water and H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide,
a different chemical with a different molar mass, so changing a subscript answers a different
problem from the one that was set. Coefficients only say how many of each substance take part, so
adjusting them balances the atoms without changing what is reacting.

flashcards.q: 8.0 g of sodium hydroxide reacts completely with sulphuric acid: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Find the mass of sodium sulphate formed. (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1, S = 32 g/mol.)
flashcards.a:
M(NaOH) = 40 g/mol, so n(NaOH) = 8.0 g ÷ 40 g/mol = 0.20 mol. The ratio NaOH : Na₂SO₄ is 2 : 1,
so n(Na₂SO₄) = 0.10 mol. M(Na₂SO₄) = 2(23) + 32 + 4(16) = 142 g/mol, so m = 0.10 mol × 142 g/mol =
14.2 g.

flashcards.q: A sample holds 1.204 × 10²⁴ particles. Find the amount in mol and state the operation used.
flashcards.a:
n = N ÷ Nₐ = 1.204 × 10²⁴ ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 2 mol. The operation is a division by the
Avogadro constant. Multiplying by 6.022 × 10⁻²³ is a different move and gives about 72.5, a number
that belongs to no unit.

flashcards.q: How many oxygen atoms are there in 0.5 mol of carbon dioxide, and how many atoms in total?
flashcards.a:
Each CO₂ molecule holds 2 oxygen atoms, so 0.5 mol of molecules holds 1 mol of oxygen atoms,
which is 6.022 × 10²³ atoms. In total each molecule holds 3 atoms, so the sample holds 1.5 mol of
atoms, which is 9.033 × 10²³ atoms.

flashcards.q: State the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP, with its unit and the conditions it applies to.
flashcards.a:
22.4 L/mol, for a gas at STP, which is 273 K and 1 atm. It applies to no solid, to no liquid,
and to no gas away from those conditions.

flashcards.q: Without notes, write the four arrows of the mole road map with the operation and the resulting unit on each one.
flashcards.a:
mass ÷ M in g/mol gives mol · mol × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ gives a bare count · mol × the
coefficient ratio from a balanced equation gives mol of another substance · mol × 22.4 L/mol gives
litres, for gases at STP only. Reversing any arrow swaps the multiplication and the division.

flashcards.q: One hand holds 1 g of hydrogen gas and the other 1 g of oxygen gas. Decide which holds more molecules and justify it with numbers. (H = 1, O = 16 g/mol.)
flashcards.a:
The hydrogen. n(H₂) = 1 g ÷ 2 g/mol = 0.5 mol against n(O₂) = 1 g ÷ 32 g/mol = 0.031 mol, so the
hydrogen holds about sixteen times as many molecules. Equal masses hold equal counts only when the
molar masses are equal.

notes.title: Mission
notes.body:
# Mission — Mole Concept

**Goal:** Solve any Class 11 stoichiometry question — mole, molar mass, empirical formula, molecular formula and equation mole ratios — unaided, with the unit written on every line.

## The exam window

| | |
|---|---|
| Next assessment | Unconfirmed — the college's terminal-exam date has not been seen yet |
| Grade 11 final | Mid-May to mid-June 2027 (Baisakh–Jestha 2084 BS) |
| Days from today | About 293 days to 15 May 2027, the earliest plausible start of that window |
| Date confidence | Low for the assessment date, medium for the final window — source is the NEB calendar pattern in `research/neb-nepal.md`, not a document from the college |

Dates marked unconfirmed are placeholders until the college calendar is seen.
An unconfirmed date is never used to move a deadline forward.

## What this unit is worth

| | |
|---|---|
| CDC unit | 2 — Stoichiometry, inside the General and Physical Chemistry domain |
| Teaching hours | 8 of 128 theory hours (the domain itself is 48 hours) |
| Usual slots in the paper | One Group A multiple-choice item and at least one Group B 5-mark calculation |
| Marks typically riding on it | Roughly 6 of 75 directly, and about 11 of 75 once the mole steps buried inside gas-law, redox and manufacture questions are counted |
| Question shapes that repeat | Percentage composition to empirical formula; empirical plus molar mass to molecular formula; mass of product from a balanced equation; number of particles or atoms from a mass |

Teaching hours are the only sanctioned weight proxy — the CDC publishes them, and the NEB
publishes no official marks weightage per unit. Do not invent chapter marks.

## Why this matters for marks

A+ needs about **67 of 75** in theory, assuming 23 of 25 in the practical. In grid terms that is
11 of 11 in Group A, about 6 of the 8 short answers close to perfect, and 2.5 of the 3 long
answers. Skipping every long answer caps the paper at 51 of 75 — a B+ however good the rest is.

For this unit specifically: the mole appears as a direct question worth about 6 marks, and as one
or two lines inside long answers on gas laws, redox titration and the industrial manufactures —
another 5 marks or so. Getting it cold is worth roughly **11 of the 75 theory marks**. It is also
the prerequisite for three later units, so a gap here is paid for four times over. Current
position across the whole paper is under 27 of 75; the distance to target is 40 marks, and this
unit is the single largest recoverable block of them at Class 11 level.

Current position on this unit: **not yet measured — no held-out question attempted**.
Target: **5 of 5 on a cold Group B stoichiometry item**. Distance: **unknown until the first
held-out attempt, which is the first thing to schedule**.

## What "done" looks like

Done is not "read the chapter". This unit is finished when all of these are true:

- [ ] All five lessons complete, including each blank-page reconstruction.
- [ ] The mindmap rebuilt from memory with no more than 3 nodes missing.
- [ ] Every flashcard for the topic has passed **3 relearning sessions**.
- [ ] The retention gates at +2 days, +7 days and +21 days are green.
- [ ] 8 cold problems solved unaided, with the unit on every line.
- [ ] One held-out past-paper question on this unit scored **5 of 5 with full working**.

Only the last line counts as proof: held-out questions are never taught from.

## Prerequisites

Three SEE-level skills this unit silently assumes, each a common hidden cause of failure here:

- **Rearranging a three-term formula.** n = m ÷ M has to become m = n × M and M = m ÷ n without
  hesitation. A gap here looks like a mole problem and is an algebra problem.
- **Ratio and proportion.** Scaling 1 : 2.5 to 2 : 5, and knowing that scaling is legal while
  rounding is not.
- **Decimal division and place value with powers of ten.** Dividing by 6.022 × 10²³ and reading
  that 0.1 of 10²³ is 10²².
- **Reading a chemical formula.** Which subscript belongs to which element, and that the subscript
  multiplies only the atom immediately before it.

Each gap gets its own backfill card set before the unit's own lessons continue.

## The lessons in this mission

- [ ] 0001 — What Is a Mole? · `lessons/0001-what-is-a-mole.html`
- [ ] 0002 — Empirical Formula from Percentage Composition · `lessons/0002-empirical-formula.html`
- [ ] 0003 — Molecular Formula from Empirical Formula · `lessons/0003-molecular-formula.html`
- [ ] 0004 — Mole Ratios from a Balanced Equation · `lessons/0004-stoichiometry-mole-ratios.html`
- [ ] 0005 — Mass, Moles and Particles: the Multi-Step Drill · `lessons/0005-mass-particles-drills.html`

Reference sheet: `reference/mole-concept-cheatsheet.html` — cumulative, printed, on the desk.

## Misconceptions this unit is known to produce

CH-M01 (mole treated as a mass), CH-M02 (equal mass read as equal moles), CH-M03 (amu and g/mol
treated as different quantities), CH-M04 (molecules, atoms, ions and formula units conflated),
CH-M06 (22.4 L/mol applied to solids, liquids or away from STP), CH-M08 (the Avogadro constant
used as a mass, or inverted to 6.022 × 10⁻²³), CH-S01 (1 : 1 mole combining assumed),
CH-S02 (mole ratio applied to grams — the single most common error in the unit),
CH-S05 (balancing by changing subscripts), CH-S06 (no particle-to-lab bridge),
CH-S08 (a ratio conflated with an amount).

A misconception that reappears three weeks after it was cleared becomes the highest-priority
review item in the system.

## Open questions — confirm, never guess

- [ ] The college's actual terminal and pre-board dates for this academic year.
- [ ] Which chemistry guidebook the class follows, and the page range for Unit 2, so the lesson
      citations can name a real source instead of declaring that none was opened.
- [ ] Whether the school's internal papers follow the post-2077 grid or still use the pre-2077
      pattern, which changes the time economics of every practice paper.
- [ ] The practical mark split for chemistry, since the 67 of 75 target assumes 23 of 25 there.
